source_text: Quas mihi ergo tu hic ambages, quae cervicalia, mendaciorum et ineptiarum, quae Hierusalem fornicanti Ezechiel propheta imputat [n28] ; admovebis, in quibus muliebres animae cubent, nomina mysteriorum tenentes, cum in ipsam divinitatem retecta profanitate commiserint. Remotis omnibus praestigiis et advocatarum saepe a te plebicularum catervis, doce iustum esse quod per Scripturas sanctas affirmare conaris.
pass_a_gloss: What windings therefore will you here move up to me, what cushions of lies and ineptitudes, which the prophet Ezekiel imputes to fornicating Jerusalem; in which womanish souls may lie, holding the names of mysteries, although they have committed with uncovered profanity against divinity itself. With all conjuring-tricks removed and the troops of little crowds often called in by you, teach that that is just which you try to affirm through the Holy Scriptures.

lemmas.lexica: LS anima; Blaise human soul as image

pass_b_english: What evasions, then, what cushions of lies and absurdities, such as the prophet Ezekiel charges against unfaithful Jerusalem, will you offer me here (Ezekiel 13:18)? On these cushions womanish souls may recline, retaining the names of sacred mysteries even though they have committed open sacrilege against divinity itself. Set aside every conjuring trick and the crowds of common folk you so often summon, and show that what you try to establish through Holy Scripture is just.

choices.why: Julian's sacred writings; keep Scripture, not 'Bible' as a later book-name.
If injustice could be proved from God's laws, divinity itself would cheapen.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
